extracted.intended_audience: Members of Parliament, English lawmakers, and the educated public concerned with press freedom and censorship
extracted.subtask_description: A 17th-century polemical pamphlet arguing against pre-publication licensing and for wide freedom of reading and printing. It sets out normative principles for what kinds of books magistrates may punish and why licensing and book-burning are harmful to learning and the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only blasphemous or libellous works warrant magistrate attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The magistrate cared to take notice of; those either blasphemous and atheistical, or libellous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton cites the practice in Athens as precedent: magistrates prosecuted only books that were 'blasphemous and atheistical, or libellous.' He gives examples (Protagoras ordered burnt for questioning the gods; laws against personal defamation) and contrasts those limited grounds with broader inquisitorial censorship. Implicit standard: official suppression should be narrowly targeted to writings that are direct blasphemy or actionable defamation, not to diverse opinions or moral laxity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to pre-publication licensing of books
rubrics_metrics.description: That no book, pamphlet, or paper shall be henceforth printed, unless the same be first approved and licensed by such, or at least one of such, as shall be thereto appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues this licensing clause (pre-publication approval) is an imported invention from the Inquisition and is dangerous and unnecessary. He claims wise commonwealths did not employ it, that it 'avails nothing to the suppressing of scandalous, seditious, and libellous books,' and that it will 'be primely to the discouragement of all learning, and the stop of truth.' Anti-patterns: imposing mandatory licensing boards, multiple imprimaturs, or clerical pre-approval before printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve books — destroying books kills reason
rubrics_metrics.description: He who destroys a good book, kills reason itself, kills the image of God, as it were in the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton frames books as living vessels of intellect ('the precious life-blood of a master spirit') and warns that burning or suppressing books is akin to homicide of reason and leads to irrevocable loss of truth. Policy implication: avoid book-burning and wholesale destruction of works; prefer correction, rebuttal, or debate to destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom for individuals to read widely and judge for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: READ ANY BOOKS WHATEVER COME TO THY HANDS, FOR THOU ART SUFFICIENT BOTH TO JUDGE ARIGHT AND TO EXAMINE EACH MATTER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton endorses trusting mature individuals to use reason and judgment when encountering texts. He invokes scriptural and patristic precedents to support allowing broad reading, arguing that knowledge of error helps discern truth. Practical guidance: rely on education, exhortation, and personal temperance rather than legal bans to regulate reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear of 'infection' from books is an insufficient ground for broad prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: First, is feared the infection that may spread; but then all human learning and controversy in religious points must remove out of the world, yea the Bible itself...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton rejects contagion-style reasoning that would ban all potentially 'infectious' writings, pointing out that such reasoning would require banning foundational texts (e.g., Bible) and ancient fathers. Standard: do not use speculative risk of moral or doctrinal 'infection' as blanket justification for censorship; instead discriminate narrowly and contextually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial works require guidance, not suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Those books, and those in great abundance, which are likeliest to taint both life and doctrine, cannot be suppressed without the fall of learning ... these books of either sort are most and soonest catching to the learned, from whom to the common people whatever is heretical or dissolute may quickly be conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton acknowledges that controversial religious works may be dangerous in untrained hands ('not to be understood without a guide') but argues the remedy is instruction and supervision by learned guides, not prohibiting the books themselves. Policy implication: invest in education, commentary, and scholarly rebuttal rather than legal bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensers cannot be presumed infallible or unbiased
rubrics_metrics.description: How shall the licensers themselves be confided in, unless we can confer upon them, or they assume to themselves above all others in the land, the grace of infallibility and uncorruptedness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton warns that empowering censors assumes an unrealistic perfection and impartiality on their part. He uses this to argue against centralized authority over printing. Anti-pattern: appointing ecclesiastical or political appointees as final arbiters of acceptable thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of opinions aids discovery of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: All opinions, yea errors, known, read, and collated, are of main service and assistance toward the speedy attainment of what is truest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing contemporary authorities (e.g., Selden) Milton asserts that exposure to varied opinions and even errors is epistemically valuable: comparing and contesting views helps refine truth. Standard for intellectual policy: encourage open debate and the circulation of differing perspectives as part of intellectual progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer exhortation and personal temperance over legal compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: God commits the managing so great a trust, without particular law or prescription, wholly to the demeanour of every grown man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton maintains moral regulation of reading is best handled by exhortation, education, and personal self-discipline, not by statute. Practical guidance: use persuasion, counsel, and institutional education to shape reading habits rather than criminalization or preemptive prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing inhibits learning and future discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be primely to the discouragement of all learning, and the stop of truth, not only by disexercising and blunting our abilities in what we know already, but by hindering and cropping the discovery that might be yet further made both in religious and civil wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues licensing dulls intellectual faculties, discourages experimentation, and prevents the development of new knowledge. Policy standard: avoid measures that systematically limit publication or impede the practice and testing of ideas if the goal is to promote learning and civic improvement.
